summary: The heart in situ inside a see-through thoracic skeleton, with the trachea, bronchial tree, larynx and thyroid gland. The four heart valves show through the translucent heart, so you can relate each valve to the sternum, ribs and intercostal spaces where it is auscultated.
clinical: Aortic area: 2nd right intercostal space at the right sternal border. Pulmonary area: 2nd left intercostal space at the left sternal border. Tricuspid area: 4th-5th left intercostal space at the lower left sternal border. Mitral area: 5th left intercostal space in the midclavicular line (apex). These are where each valve's sounds carry best, downstream of flow, not where the valves lie: all four sit behind the sternum.

S1 is closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of ventricular systole and is loudest at the apex. S2 is closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole and is loudest at the base; it splits physiologically on inspiration because the pulmonary valve closes later.

Heart.name: Heart and great vessels
Heart.description: The heart with the superior and inferior venae cavae, the aorta (ascending, arch and descending thoracic), the pulmonary trunk and arteries and the pulmonary veins, made see-through to show the valves. It lies in the middle mediastinum, two-thirds left of the midline, with its apex near the left 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line.

Valves.name: Heart valves
Valves.description: All four valves: the pulmonary valve (most anterior and superior, behind the left 3rd costal cartilage), the aortic valve (behind the left half of the sternum at the 3rd intercostal space), the tricuspid valve (behind the right half of the sternum at the 4th intercostal space) and the mitral valve (behind the left half of the sternum at the 4th costal cartilage), both with their chordae tendineae. The valves lie close together behind the sternum, which is why each is best heard away from its anatomical position.
structures: Posterior leaflet of left atrioventricular valve

Trachea.name: Trachea and bronchial tree
Trachea.description: The trachea runs from the cricoid cartilage (C6) to its bifurcation at the carina (sternal angle, T4-T5), then branches into main, lobar and segmental bronchi. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left, so inhaled foreign bodies usually lodge on the right.

Tracheal cartilages.name: Tracheal and bronchial cartilages
Tracheal cartilages.description: C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings, open posteriorly where the trachealis muscle closes the gap, keep the trachea and bronchi open. In the smaller bronchi the rings give way to irregular cartilage plates.

Lungs.name: Lungs
Lungs.description: The right lung has three lobes and the left two, with the cardiac notch of the left lung exposing the heart's anterior surface. Kept almost invisible here so the heart and bronchial tree stay in view.

Htc.name: Hyoid bone, thyroid and cricoid cartilages
Htc.description: The hyoid bone (C3), the shield-shaped thyroid cartilage with its superior and inferior horns (C4-C5), and the ring-shaped cricoid cartilage (C6), the only complete ring in the airway. The cricothyroid membrane between thyroid and cricoid is the site of emergency cricothyroidotomy.

Ligament.name: Thyrohyoid membrane
Ligament.description: Fibroelastic sheet from the upper border of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone, thickened at its free posterior edges as the lateral thyrohyoid ligaments. The internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels pierce it.

Thyroid gland.name: Thyroid gland
Thyroid gland.description: Two lobes joined by an isthmus that crosses the 2nd-4th tracheal rings below the cricoid cartilage. Enclosed in pretracheal fascia, it moves up with the larynx on swallowing, a useful sign for telling a thyroid swelling from other neck lumps.

Thorax.name: Thoracic skeleton
Thorax.description: Sternum, ribs, thoracic vertebrae, clavicles, scapulae and the heads of the humeri. For auscultation, count intercostal spaces from the sternal angle, where the 2nd costal cartilage joins the sternum; the space below the 2nd rib is the 2nd intercostal space.

Costal cartilages.name: Costal cartilages
Costal cartilages.description: Hyaline cartilage bars joining the ribs to the sternum: ribs 1-7 directly, ribs 8-10 through the cartilage above to form the costal margin, and ribs 11-12 end free. Their flexibility lets the chest wall move in breathing.

Vertebral discs.name: Intervertebral discs
Vertebral discs.description: Fibrocartilaginous discs between the vertebral bodies, each an outer anulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus. Thoracic discs are thin and the region is splinted by the ribs, so thoracic disc herniation is uncommon.

notes: Despite the title, the file contains no auscultation-point markers: 'Htc' is the hyoid bone plus thyroid and cricoid cartilages (confirmed on close renders), and the auscultation sites were presumably Sketchfab annotations, which the download does not include. They are covered in the clinical notes instead. The source file sets the lungs, thorax, costal cartilages and discs fully transparent (alpha 0); they are shown faintly here to give the rib and intercostal-space landmarks for auscultation. The 'Heart' mesh includes the great vessels and cannot be split into chambers. The valves are a single mesh, so the four valves cannot be selected separately. The mitral valve links to 'Posterior leaflet of left atrioventricular valve' because the atlas has no whole mitral valve entry. 'Ligament' identified as the thyrohyoid membrane from its position between hyoid and thyroid cartilage with lateral thickenings; its lower edge runs a little way behind the thyroid laminae in the mesh.
